title: Semibounded forms, variational spectra and Birman–Schwinger

items.title: Semibounded closed-form representation and perturbation
items.design_state: Assigned design item; complete current statement and argument are recorded in its item carrier.
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert space, let $Q\subseteq H$ be a dense linear subspace, and let
$q:Q\times Q\to\mathbb C$ be a symmetric sesquilinear form, linear in its
first variable. Write $q[u]=q(u,u)$. Suppose that for some $c\ge0$,
$q[u]\ge-c\|u\|^2$ for every $u\in Q$, and that $Q$ is complete in the form
norm $\|u\|_{q,c}^2=q[u]+(c+1)\|u\|^2$. Then there is a unique self-adjoint
operator $H_q\ge-cI$ such that
$$D((H_q+cI)^{1/2})=Q,\qquad q(u,v)=\langle H_qu,v\rangle\quad(u\in D(H_q),\ v\in Q).$$
Equivalently, $D(H_q)$ consists exactly of those $u\in Q$ for which there is
$f\in H$ satisfying $q(u,v)=\langle f,v\rangle$ for all $v\in Q$, and then
$H_qu=f$. Under the $e^{tA}$ generator convention for associated forms, the
associated operator is $A=-H_q$. If $q_0$ is a densely defined closed symmetric
form with $q_0[u]\ge0$ and $v$ is a symmetric sesquilinear form on $Q(q_0)$
satisfying
$$|v[u,u]|\le a q_0[u]+b\|u\|^2\quad(u\in Q(q_0)),\qquad 0\le a<1,\ b\ge0,$$
then $q_0+v$ is closed and bounded below by $-b$ on the same domain. It has a
unique self-adjoint representing operator there. The form bound is not an
operator-relative bound.
items.proof_route: Apply Riesz to the shifted closed form to construct a bounded positive injective resolvent, invert it by spectral calculus, identify the represented operator domain, and prove the form perturbation by equivalent shifted norms.

references.title: Marcello Porta, Mathematical Quantum Theory, University of Tübingen lecture notes (2019)
references.locator: Section 4.4, Theorem 4.65 and its proof, printed pp.41-42: unique self-adjoint representation of a densely defined closed semibounded form and the represented operator domain.

references.title: Phan Thanh Nam, Functional Analysis II, lecture notes, Winter 2020-2021, Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität München
references.locator: Chapter 2, §2.2, printed pp.14-16: Friedrichs extension and the semibounded quadratic-form domain; used as related form-method background.

items.strategy:
**Given:** [A1] and the form data in the Statement. Use inner products linear
in the first variable throughout.

1.1 If $H=\{0\}$, density forces $Q=\{0\}$ and the zero operator is the unique self-adjoint representation; the perturbation conclusion is the same. Hence assume $H\ne\{0\}$. [given]

1.2 Put $\mathfrak a(u,v)=q(u,v)+(c+1)\langle u,v\rangle$ on $Q$. The lower bound gives $\mathfrak a[u]\ge\|u\|^2$, so $\mathfrak a$ is positive definite; its norm is exactly $\|\cdot\|_{q,c}$, hence $(Q,\mathfrak a)$ is a Hilbert space. The inclusion $J:Q\to H$ is injective, bounded with $\|J\|\le1$, and has dense range. [F1, given]

2.1 For each $f\in H$, Cauchy–Schwarz [F4] and $\|J\|\le1$ make $v\mapsto\langle Jv,f\rangle$ a bounded linear functional on $(Q,\mathfrak a)$. Apply [F2] and let $J^*f\in Q$ be its unique representing vector: $\mathfrak a(v,J^*f)=\langle Jv,f\rangle$ for every $v\in Q$. Uniqueness makes $f\mapsto J^*f$ linear. Define $R:=JJ^*:H\to H$. Taking $v=J^*f$ gives $\|J^*f\|_{q,c}^2=\langle Rf,f\rangle$, and $\|Rf\|\le\|J^*f\|_{q,c}$; therefore $\|J^*f\|_{q,c}\le\|f\|$ and $\|R\|\le1$. [A1, F2, F4, step 1.2, construct]

3.1 For $f,g\in H$, the defining identity and symmetry of $\mathfrak a$ give $\langle Rf,g\rangle=\mathfrak a(J^*f,J^*g)=\langle f,Rg\rangle$, while $\langle Rf,f\rangle=\|J^*f\|_{q,c}^2\ge0$; hence $R$ is bounded, positive, self-adjoint, and $R\le I$. If $Rf=0$, then $J^*f=0$, so $\langle Jv,f\rangle=0$ for dense $J(Q)$ and thus $f=0$; consequently $\ker R=\{0\}$ and $\operatorname{ran}R$ is dense. [step 2.1, given, algebra]

4.1 The bounded positive operator $R$ has a positive square root by [F3]. On $\operatorname{ran}R^{1/2}$ define $U_0(R^{1/2}f)=J^*f$. This is well-defined because $R^{1/2}$ is injective, and $\|J^*f\|_{q,c}^2=\langle Rf,f\rangle=\|R^{1/2}f\|^2$, so $U_0$ is an isometry. Both its domain and range are dense: the first because $\ker R^{1/2}=0$, the second because a vector in $Q$ orthogonal to all $J^*f$ has image under $J$ orthogonal to every $f\in H$ and is therefore zero. Thus $U_0$ extends to a unitary $U:H\to(Q,\mathfrak a)$; taking adjoints in $J^*=UR^{1/2}$ yields $J=R^{1/2}U^*$. Hence $J(Q)=\operatorname{ran}R^{1/2}$ and $\|u\|_{q,c}=\|R^{-1/2}Ju\|$ for every $u\in Q$. [step 2.1, step 3.1, F3, algebra]

5.1 By [F3], define $T=R^{-1}$ by the Borel function $s\mapsto s^{-1}$ on $s>0$ (its value at $0$ is immaterial because $\ker R=0$). Then $T$ is self-adjoint, $T\ge I$, $D(T)=\operatorname{ran}R$, and $D(T^{1/2})=\operatorname{ran}R^{1/2}$. Put $H_q=T-(c+1)I$. It is self-adjoint and $H_q\ge-cI$. Step 4.1 gives $D((H_q+cI)^{1/2})=D((T-I)^{1/2})=D(T^{1/2})=J(Q)$, since the spectral weights $s-1$ and $s$ on $[1,\infty)$ are integrable for exactly the same vectors. [step 3.1, step 4.1, F3, algebra]

6.1 The unitary $U^*:Q\to H$ satisfies $U^*u=R^{-1/2}Ju=T^{1/2}Ju$ by step 4.1. Therefore $\mathfrak a(u,v)=\langle T^{1/2}Ju,T^{1/2}Jv\rangle$ for all $u,v\in Q$. If $u\in D(T)$ and $v\in Q$, the spectral calculus gives $\langle T^{1/2}Ju,T^{1/2}Jv\rangle=\langle TJu,Jv\rangle$; subtracting $(c+1)\langle Ju,Jv\rangle$ proves $q(u,v)=\langle H_qu,Jv\rangle$. Conversely, if $q(u,v)=\langle g,Jv\rangle$ for every $v\in Q$, then $\mathfrak a(u,v)=\langle g+(c+1)Ju,Jv\rangle$, so the uniqueness in the Riesz construction gives $u=J^*(g+(c+1)Ju)$ and $Ju=R(g+(c+1)Ju)\in D(T)$; the representing vector is $g=H_qu$. This proves the stated operator domain. The resolvent $(H_q+(c+1)I)^{-1}=R$ is uniquely determined by the form's Riesz equation, so no other self-adjoint operator can represent $q$. [step 2.1, step 4.1, step 5.1, F2, F3]

7.1 Now let $q_0$ and $v$ satisfy the perturbation hypotheses, and choose $C>b+1$. Then $(1-a)q_0[u]+(C-b)\|u\|^2\le(q_0+v)[u]+C\|u\|^2\le(1+a)q_0[u]+(C+b)\|u\|^2$. Since $1-a>0$ and $C-b>1$, this shifted form norm is bounded above and below by positive multiples of the complete norm $q_0[u]+\|u\|^2$. Also $(q_0+v)[u]\ge-b\|u\|^2$. Set $N_C=(q_0+v)[u]+C\|u\|^2$ and $N_{b+1}=(q_0+v)[u]+(b+1)\|u\|^2$. Then $N_C\ge(C-b)\|u\|^2$ and $N_{b+1}=N_C-(C-b-1)\|u\|^2\ge N_C/(C-b)$, while $N_{b+1}\le N_C$. Thus the defining shift $b+1$ norm is equivalent and complete, so $q_0+v$ is closed with lower bound $-b$. Applying the representation argument in steps 1.2, 2.1, 3.1, 4.1, 5.1, and 6.1 with lower bound $-b$ gives its unique self-adjoint representing operator bounded below by $-b$. [given, step 1.2, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 4.1, step 5.1, step 6.1, algebra] ∎

items.title: Rank-one resolvent and bound-state equation
items.design_state: Assigned design item; complete current statement and argument are recorded in its item carrier.
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $H_0$ be a self-adjoint operator on a complex
Hilbert space $H$, with inner product linear in its first variable and
$\inf\sigma(H_0)>-\infty$. Let $g\in H$, $\lambda\in\mathbb R$, and define
$P_g:H\to H$ by $P_gf=\langle f,g\rangle g$. Put
$H_\lambda=H_0+\lambda P_g$ on $D(H_\lambda)=D(H_0)$ and
$R_0(z)=(H_0-zI)^{-1}$. Then $H_\lambda$ is self-adjoint. For every
$z\in\rho(H_0)$ such that
$d_\lambda(z):=1+\lambda\langle R_0(z)g,g\rangle\ne0$, one has
$z\in\rho(H_\lambda)$ and
$$R_\lambda(z):=(H_\lambda-zI)^{-1}=R_0(z)-\frac{\lambda R_0(z)P_gR_0(z)}{1+\lambda\langle R_0(z)g,g\rangle}.$$
For real $E<\inf\sigma(H_0)$ and $g\ne0$, $E$ is an eigenvalue of $H_\lambda$
if and only if $d_\lambda(E)=0$; in that case the eigenspace is one-dimensional.
items.proof_route: Prove self-adjointness by bounded symmetric perturbation; reduce the resolvent inverse to X²=mX, multiply the proposed inverse on both sides, and derive the below-threshold eigenvalue condition and eigenspace dimension.

references.title: S. Albeverio and P. Kurasov, Singular Perturbations of Differential Operators: Solvable Schrödinger Type Operators
references.locator: Chapter 1, §1.1.1, Theorem 1.1.1 and proof, printed pp.9-10: rank-one resolvent formula for a bounded perturbation of a possibly unbounded self-adjoint operator.

references.title: Phan Thanh Nam, Functional Analysis II, lecture notes, Winter 2020-2021, Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität München
references.locator: Chapter 2, §2.2, printed pp.14-15: Kato-Rellich theorem used for the bounded symmetric perturbation interface.

items.strategy:
**Given:** [A1], [A2], $P_gf=\langle f,g\rangle g$, and the operators in the
Statement.

1.1 For every $f\in H$, [F2] gives $\|P_gf\|=|\langle f,g\rangle|\|g\|\le\|g\|^2\|f\|$. Also $\langle P_gf,h\rangle=\langle f,g\rangle\langle g,h\rangle =\langle f,P_gh\rangle$, so $P_g$ is bounded and self-adjoint, including $g=0$. Thus $\lambda P_g$ is symmetric on $D(H_0)$ with relative bound zero; [F1] implies that $H_\lambda$ is self-adjoint on $D(H_0)$. [A2, F1, F2, given]

1.2 Fix $z\in\rho(H_0)$ and write $R_0=R_0(z)$, $m=\langle R_0g,g\rangle$, and $X=R_0P_g$. Then $Xf=\langle f,g\rangle R_0g$ and $X^2f=\langle f,g\rangle\langle R_0g,g\rangle R_0g=mXf$; hence $X^2=mX$. If $d=1+\lambda m\ne0$, direct multiplication gives $(I+\lambda X)^{-1}=I-\lambda X/d$. [A1, given, algebra]

2.1 Define $S=(I-\lambda X/d)R_0$. Its range is contained in $D(H_0)$. Since $P_gR_0P_g=mP_g$, on $D(H_0)$ one has $S(H_\lambda-zI)=(I-\lambda X/d)(I+\lambda X)=I$. On $H$ one has $(H_\lambda-zI)S=I-\lambda P_gR_0/d+\lambda P_gR_0 -\lambda^2mP_gR_0/d=I$, using $d=1+\lambda m$. Thus $S$ is a bounded two-sided inverse from $H$ onto $D(H_\lambda)$, and its expansion is the stated resolvent formula. [step 1.2, A1, algebra]

3.1 Let $E<\inf\sigma(H_0)$ be real. By [A1], $R_0(E)$ exists. If $H_\lambda u=Eu$ with $u\ne0$, then $u=-\lambda\langle u,g\rangle R_0(E)g$. The coefficient $\langle u,g\rangle$ cannot be zero, because that would give $u=0$; applying $\langle\cdot,g\rangle$ therefore yields $1+\lambda\langle R_0(E)g,g\rangle=0$. Conversely, if this scalar is zero, then $u=R_0(E)g\ne0$ and $(H_\lambda-EI)u=g+\lambda\langle R_0(E)g,g\rangle g=0$. Every eigenvector satisfies the same scalar-multiple formula for $R_0(E)g$, so the eigenspace is one-dimensional. [A1, step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra] ∎

items.title: Free Laplacian form domain and realization
items.design_state: Scaffolder-added local A-page prerequisite; complete proof authored in this batch.
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. On
$H=L^2(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C)$ use the unitary Fourier transform
$\widehat u(\xi)=\int_{\mathbb R^3}e^{-2\pi i x\cdot\xi}u(x)\,dx$ on
$L^1\cap L^2$. Let $H_0=-\Delta$ be the self-adjoint multiplier
$\mathcal F_2^*M_{4\pi^2|\xi|^2}\mathcal F_2$ with domain
$D(H_0)=W^{2,2}(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C)$. Put
$Q_0=W^{1,2}(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C)$ and
$$q_0(u,v)=\sum_{j=1}^3\langle \partial_j u,\partial_j v\rangle_{L^2}\quad(u,v\in Q_0),$$
where $\partial_j$ are weak derivatives. Then $q_0$ is dense, symmetric,
nonnegative, and closed; its associated self-adjoint operator is exactly $H_0$,
with $Q(H_0)=D(H_0^{1/2})=Q_0$ and
$$q_0(u,v)=\langle H_0u,v\rangle\quad(u\in D(H_0),\ v\in Q_0).$$
items.proof_route: Use the fixed 2π Fourier convention to identify the weak-derivative form, establish density and closedness, and recover the operator domain distributionally as W^{2,2}.

references.title: Phan Thanh Nam, Functional Analysis II, lecture notes, Winter 2020-2021, Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität München
references.locator: Chapter 2, §2.5, printed pp.25-27: the free Schrödinger operator on H² and its quadratic-form domain.

references.title: Marcello Porta, Mathematical Quantum Theory, University of Tübingen lecture notes (2019)
references.locator: Sections 3.1 and 3.6, printed pp.7-8 and 23-24: Fourier transform convention and unitary L² extension used in the free-operator calculation.

items.strategy:
**Given:** [A1] and the Hilbert space, Fourier transform, weak derivatives,
and free multiplier stated above.

1.1 Define $q_0$ on $Q_0=W^{1,2}$ by the displayed weak-derivative pairing. By [F2], for $u,v\in Q_0$, $$q_0(u,v)=\int_{\mathbb R^3}4\pi^2|\xi|^2\widehat u(\xi)\overline{\widehat v(\xi)}\,d\xi.$$ Thus $q_0$ is sesquilinear, symmetric and nonnegative. Moreover $q_0[u]+\|u\|_2^2=\|u\|_{W^{1,2}}^2$, which is complete by [F3], so $q_0$ is closed by [F4]. Since Schwartz functions lie in $Q_0$ and are dense in $L^2$ by [F5], $Q_0$ is dense. [A1, F2, F3, F4, F5, algebra]

1.2 If $u\in D(H_0)=W^{2,2}$ and $v\in Q_0$, Plancherel [F2] and Cauchy–Schwarz [F6] give $q_0(u,v)=\int4\pi^2|\xi|^2\widehat u\,\overline{\widehat v} =\langle H_0u,v\rangle$; both factors in this pairing are in $L^2$ by the $W^{2,2}$ and $W^{1,2}$ hypotheses. [F1, F2, F3, F6, given]

1.3 Conversely, suppose $u\in Q_0$ and $f\in H$ satisfy $q_0(u,v)=\langle f,v\rangle$ for every $v\in Q_0$. Testing with Schwartz $v$ and using Plancherel gives $\int(4\pi^2|\xi|^2\widehat u(\xi)-\widehat f(\xi))\overline{\widehat v(\xi)}\,d\xi=0$. The Fourier transform maps Schwartz space onto itself by [F5], so the locally integrable distribution $4\pi^2|\xi|^2\widehat u-\widehat f$ vanishes; therefore $|\xi|^2\widehat u\in L^2$. By [F3], $u\in W^{2,2}=D(H_0)$, and [F1] then gives $H_0u=f$. Thus the form-associated operator domain and action are exactly those of $H_0$. [F1, F2, F3, F4, F5, given]

2.1 Steps 1.2-1.3 show that the nonnegative self-adjoint operator $H_0$ is the operator represented by the dense closed form $q_0$. Uniqueness in [F4] therefore gives $Q(H_0)=D(H_0^{1/2})=Q_0$, completing the Statement. [F1, F4, step 1.1, step 1.2, step 1.3] ∎

items.title: Form min-max below the essential spectrum
items.design_state: Assigned design item; complete current statement and argument are recorded in its item carrier.
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Let $H\ne\{0\}$ be a complex Hilbert space and
let $A$ be a self-adjoint operator with $A\ge-cI$ for some $c\ge0$. Let
$E_A$ be its spectral projection-valued measure, let
$Q(A)=D((A+cI)^{1/2})$, and define the associated form by
$$q_A[u]=\|(A+cI)^{1/2}u\|^2-c\|u\|^2\quad(u\in Q(A)).$$
Set $\alpha=\inf\sigma_{\mathrm{ess}}(A)$, with $\alpha=+\infty$ when the
essential spectrum is empty. For each integer $k\ge1$, put
$$\lambda_k(A)=\inf_{\substack{L\subseteq Q(A)\text{ linear},\ \dim L=k}}\ \sup_{\substack{u\in L\\\|u\|=1}}q_A[u],$$
where the infimum of an empty family is $+\infty$. Then $\lambda_k(A)$ is the
$k$th eigenvalue below $\alpha$, counted with multiplicity, when at least $k$
such eigenvalues exist; otherwise $\lambda_k(A)=\alpha$. If the inclusion
$Q(A)\hookrightarrow H$ is compact in the form norm
$\|u\|_{Q(A)}^2=q_A[u]+(c+1)\|u\|^2$, then $A$ has a complete orthonormal
eigenbasis; every eigenvalue has finite multiplicity, and the only possible
accumulation is at $+\infty$.
items.proof_route: Compare dimensions of spectral projections with finite-dimensional form subspaces; use the PVM for the essential-spectrum threshold and compact embedding for a compact shifted resolvent.

references.title: Phan Thanh Nam, Functional Analysis II, lecture notes, Winter 2020-2021, Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität München
references.locator: Chapter 2, §2.3, printed pp.17-18: min-max theorem, essential-spectrum threshold, proof, and compact-resolvent eigenbasis criterion.

items.strategy:
**Given:** [A1] and the operator, PVM, and form in the Statement.

1.1 By Choice [A1], [F1] and the spectral calculus give, for $u\in Q(A)$, $q_A[u]=\int\lambda\,dE_u(\lambda)$; the lower bound ensures this integral is finite after the stated shift. The form norm in the Statement is exactly $\|(A+(c+1)I)^{1/2}u\|$. [A1, F1, F3, given]

1.2 Fix $t<\alpha$. Since $A\ge-cI$, the spectral points in $(-\infty,t]$ lie in the compact interval $[-c,t]$. If this interval contained infinitely many spectral points, compactness of the interval and closedness of $\sigma(A)$ would give an accumulation point $s\le t$ in $\sigma(A)$. Such an accumulation point is essential by [F2], contradicting $s\le t<\alpha$. Thus there are finitely many spectral points below $t$, each isolated with finite multiplicity. By [F3], $E_A((-\infty,t))$ is supported on their eigenspaces, so it has finite rank. [F2, F3, given, algebra]

1.3 Now assume the form-domain inclusion is compact. The map $(A+(c+1)I)^{-1}:H\to Q(A)$ is bounded because $\|(A+(c+1)I)^{1/2}(A+(c+1)I)^{-1}f\|\le\|f\|$ by [F3]. Composing with the compact inclusion $Q(A)\hookrightarrow H$ shows that this resolvent is compact by [F5]. It is positive, self-adjoint and injective. By [F4], its nonzero eigenspaces have finite dimension and span $H$. On each such subspace, $A=(A+(c+1)I)- (c+1)I$ has eigenvalue $r^{-1}-(c+1)$ when the resolvent eigenvalue is $r>0$. The compact spectral theorem says these $r$ can accumulate only at zero; therefore the resulting eigenvalues of $A$ have finite multiplicity and can accumulate only at $+\infty$. This proves the compact-embedding conclusion. [F3, F4, F5, given, algebra]

2.1 Define $\nu_k=\inf\{t\in\mathbb R:\operatorname{rank}E_A((-\infty,t))\ge k\}$, with $\inf\emptyset=+\infty$. If there are at least $k$ eigenvalues below $\alpha$, their finite-rank spectral projections show that $\nu_k$ is the $k$th such eigenvalue counted with multiplicity. If fewer exist, no $t<\alpha$ has rank at least $k$. When $\alpha<\infty$, closedness of $\sigma_{\mathrm{ess}}(A)$ gives $\alpha\in\sigma_{\mathrm{ess}}(A)$, so every $t>\alpha$ contains an interval about $\alpha$ inside $(-\infty,t)$ whose spectral projection has infinite rank by [F2]; hence $\nu_k=\alpha$. When $\alpha=+\infty$, the spectrum consists only of discrete eigenvalues; if fewer than $k$ exist, their finite-dimensional eigenspaces span $H$ by [F3], so $\dim H<k$, no $k$-dimensional subspace exists, and $\nu_k=+\infty$. Thus $\nu_k$ has exactly the target value in every case. [F2, F3, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 Let $L\subset Q(A)$ have dimension $k$, and set $m_L=\sup_{u\in L,\,\|u\|=1}q_A[u]$. By finite-dimensional Gram--Schmidt, choose an orthonormal basis $e_1,\ldots,e_k$ of $L$. For a unit vector $u=\sum_i a_i e_i$, each $|a_i|\le1$ and $q_A[u]=\sum_{i,j}a_i\overline{a_j}q_A(e_i,e_j)$, so $|q_A[u]|\le\sum_{i,j}|q_A(e_i,e_j)|<\infty$ uniformly on the unit sphere. Thus $m_L<\infty$. For any $t>m_L$, if $\operatorname{rank}E_A(( -\infty,t))<k$, the projection restricted to $L$ has a nonzero kernel; choose a unit $u\in L$ with $E_A(( -\infty,t))u=0$. Its spectral measure is supported in $[t,\infty)$, so [F1] gives $q_A[u]\ge t>m_L$, a contradiction. Hence $\operatorname{rank}E_A(( -\infty,t))\ge k$, so $\nu_k\le t$ for every $t>m_L$ and therefore $\nu_k\le m_L$. Taking the infimum over $L$ yields $\nu_k\le\lambda_k(A)$. [F1, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 If $\nu_k<\infty$ and $t>\nu_k$, monotonicity of the interval projections gives some $s<t$ with $\operatorname{rank}E_A((-\infty,s))\ge k$. Choose a $k$-dimensional subspace $L$ of this range. Its spectral support is bounded below by $-c$ and above by $s$, hence $L\subset Q(A)$; [F1] also gives $q_A[u]\le s\|u\|^2$ on $L$. Thus $\lambda_k(A)\le s<t$; letting $t$ decrease to $\nu_k$ gives $\lambda_k(A)\le\nu_k$. If $\nu_k=+\infty$, Step 2.1 shows $\dim H<k$, so the variational infimum is also $+\infty$. Combining with Step 3.1 gives $\lambda_k(A)=\nu_k$, proving the min-max identity and its spectral interpretation. [F1, F3, step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 Steps 1.1-4.1 establish the form min-max characterization, including the essential-spectrum threshold and the empty-spectrum convention; Step 1.3 proves the complete discrete eigenbasis under compact form-domain embedding. [step 1.1, step 1.2, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 4.1, step 1.3] ∎

items.title: Yukawa kernel of the free resolvent in three dimensions
items.design_state: Scaffolder-added local A-page prerequisite; complete proof authored in this batch.
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. On
$L^2(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C)$ use
$\widehat f(\xi)=\int e^{-2\pi i x\cdot\xi}f(x)\,dx$ and the unitary
extension $\mathcal F_2$. For $\kappa>0$, let
$$G_\kappa(x)=\frac{e^{-\kappa|x|}}{4\pi|x|}\quad(x\ne0),$$
with any value at $x=0$. Then $G_\kappa\in L^1\cap L^2$, and
$$\widehat G_\kappa(\xi)=\frac1{4\pi^2|\xi|^2+\kappa^2}.$$
Consequently convolution by $G_\kappa$ is the bounded operator
$(-\Delta+\kappa^2)^{-1}$ on $L^2$, with its convolution integral interpreted
in the usual almost-everywhere $L^2$ sense.
items.proof_route: Integrate the radial Fourier transform explicitly, establish L¹ and L² integrability, and extend the convolution multiplier identity from Schwartz functions to L².

references.title: Phan Thanh Nam, Functional Analysis II, lecture notes, Winter 2020-2021, Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität München
references.locator: Chapter 3, §3.3, printed pp.45-47: Fourier-side free resolvent and three-dimensional Yukawa kernel.

items.strategy:
**Given:** [A1], [F1], [F2], [F3], and $\kappa>0$.

1.1 Spherical coordinates give $$\|G_\kappa\|_1=\int_0^\infty r e^{-\kappa r}\,dr=\kappa^{-2},\qquad \|G_\kappa\|_2^2=\frac1{4\pi}\int_0^\infty e^{-2\kappa r}\,dr =\frac1{8\pi\kappa}.$$ Thus both norms are finite; the point value at the origin does not affect the $L^p$ class. [given, algebra]

2.1 For $\rho=|\xi|>0$, [F1] and the elementary integral $\int_0^\infty e^{-\kappa r}\sin(ar)\,dr=a/(\kappa^2+a^2)$ for $a>0$ give $$\widehat G_\kappa(\xi)=\frac1{2\pi\rho}\int_0^\infty e^{-\kappa r}\sin(2\pi\rho r)\,dr =\frac1{\kappa^2+4\pi^2\rho^2}.$$ At $\xi=0$, direct integration gives $\widehat G_\kappa(0)=\int_0^\infty r e^{-\kappa r}\,dr=\kappa^{-2}$, the same formula. [F1, step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 Put $M=\|G_\kappa\|_1>0$ and $A(x)=\int G_\kappa(y)|f(x-y)|^2dy$. Tonelli and translation invariance [F2, F3] give $\int A(x)dx=M\|f\|_2^2$, so $A(x)<\infty$ for almost every $x$. For each such $x$, $\int G_\kappa(y)|f(x-y)|dy\le(M+A(x))/2<\infty$ by $2t\le1+t^2$, so define $b(x)=\int G_\kappa(y)f(x-y)dy$. Expanding the nonnegative integral $\int G_\kappa(y)|f(x-y)-b(x)/M|^2dy$ gives $0\le A(x)-|b(x)|^2/M$, hence $|b(x)|^2\le M A(x)$. Integrating yields $\|G_\kappa*f\|_2^2\le M^2\|f\|_2^2$. Therefore convolution is defined almost everywhere and gives a bounded operator on $L^2$. [F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 If $f$ is Schwartz, then $G_\kappa*f\in L^1$ by Fubini and translation invariance [F3], and lies in $L^2$ by step 2.2. Fubini in the ordinary Fourier integral gives $\mathcal F(G_\kappa*f)=\widehat G_\kappa\widehat f$; Plancherel identifies this with the $L^2$ transform. Since $|\widehat G_\kappa(\xi)|\le\|G_\kappa\|_1$ by the integral definition of the Fourier transform, multiplication by $\widehat G_\kappa$ is bounded on $L^2$. Schwartz density and boundedness of convolution therefore extend the identity to all $f\in L^2$. [A1, F2, F3, step 1.1, step 2.2, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 By [A1], $-\Delta$ is the multiplier $4\pi^2|\xi|^2$. Therefore $(4\pi^2|\xi|^2+\kappa^2)^{-1}$ is the bounded inverse multiplier of $-\Delta+\kappa^2$; its product with the latter multiplier is $1$, and its range lies in the operator domain because $4\pi^2|\xi|^2/(4\pi^2|\xi|^2+\kappa^2)\le1$. Step 3.1 identifies the same multiplier for convolution, so convolution is exactly $(-\Delta+\kappa^2)^{-1}$. [A1, step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

items.title: Birman–Schwinger principle for bounded compactly supported potentials
items.design_state: Assigned design item; complete current statement and argument are recorded in its item carrier.
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Let
$W:\mathbb R^3\to[0,\infty)$ be measurable, essentially bounded, and zero
almost everywhere outside a compact set $S$. Put $s(x)=\sqrt{W(x)}$ almost
everywhere. On $L^2=L^2(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C)$, let
$M_s,M_W:L^2\to L^2$ be the multiplication operators $(M_sf)(x)=s(x)f(x)$
and $(M_Wf)(x)=W(x)f(x)$, interpreted as almost-everywhere classes. These are
bounded nonnegative self-adjoint operators with $M_s^2=M_W$ and
$\|M_s\|^2,\|M_W\|\le\|W\|_{L^\infty}$. Let $H_0=-\Delta$ be the free
Laplacian with domain
$D(H_0)=W^{2,2}(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C)$, and set
$H=H_0-M_W$ on $D(H_0)$. For $\kappa>0$ define
$$K_\kappa=M_s(H_0+\kappa^2 I)^{-1}M_s.$$
Then $H$ is self-adjoint and bounded below, and $K_\kappa$ is positive,
self-adjoint, and compact, with integral kernel
$$s(x)\frac{e^{-\kappa|x-y|}}{4\pi|x-y|}s(y).$$
The eigenspaces at $-\kappa^2$ for $H$ and at $1$ for $K_\kappa$ are linearly
isomorphic. Moreover, the finite number of eigenvalues of $H$ strictly below
$-\kappa^2$, counted with multiplicity, equals the finite number of
eigenvalues of $K_\kappa$ strictly greater than $1$, counted with
multiplicity.
items.proof_route: Prove the Yukawa-weighted kernel is square-integrable and compact; intertwine threshold eigenvectors and transform the shifted form through (−Δ+κ²)^{1/2} to compare negative index with eigenvalues above one.

references.title: Phan Thanh Nam, Functional Analysis II, lecture notes, Winter 2020-2021, Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität München
references.locator: Chapter 3, §3.3, printed pp.42-45: Birman-Schwinger correspondence, compactness, and eigenvalue counting. The notes use an inclusive endpoint convention; this item proves the strict-below cutoff stated here.

items.strategy:
**Given:** [A1], [A2], and the potential, operators, and parameter in the
Statement.

1.1 Multiplication by $W$ is bounded, nonnegative, and symmetric. Kato–Rellich therefore makes $H=H_0-W$ self-adjoint on $H^2$, with $H\ge-MI$, where $M=\|W\|_\infty$. On $H^1$ define $q_H(u,v)=q_0(u,v)-\langle su,sv\rangle$. Its perturbation has form bound $a=0$, $b=M$, so [F1] makes it closed and bounded below by $-M$. [A1, A2, F1, algebra]

2.1 Let $\widetilde H$ be the self-adjoint operator representing $q_H$ from [F1]. For $u\in H^2$ and $v\in H^1$, the free-form identity [A1] and $\langle su,sv\rangle=\langle Wu,v\rangle$ give $q_H(u,v)=\langle(H_0-W)u,v\rangle$. Thus $H\subseteq\widetilde H$; self-adjointness gives $\widetilde H\subseteq H^*=H$, so $\widetilde H=H$. The representation theorem's square-root identity on the full form domain, with shift $M+1$, and [F3] then identify $q_H$ with the spectral form of $H$. [A1, F1, F3, step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 The resolvent convolution formula in [F2] gives, for a.e. $x$,
$(K_\kappa f)(x)=s(x)\int G_\kappa(x-y)s(y)f(y)\,dy$; thus the displayed
function is the integral kernel of $K_\kappa$. If $S$ is a compact set outside
which $W=0$ almost everywhere and $M=\|W\|_\infty$, then
$$\iint |s(x)G_\kappa(x-y)s(y)|^2\,dx\,dy\le M^2|S|\int_{S-S}|G_\kappa(z)|^2\,dz<\infty,$$
because $S-S$ is bounded and the $|z|^{-1}$ singularity of $G_\kappa$ is
square-integrable locally in three dimensions. This is an $L^2$ kernel, so
[F5] makes its integral operator $K_\kappa$ Hilbert–Schmidt and compact.
[F2, F5, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 With $R_\kappa=(H_0+\kappa^2)^{-1}$, $K_\kappa=(sR_\kappa^{1/2})(sR_\kappa^{1/2})^*$, so it is positive and self-adjoint. Here $R_\kappa^{1/2}$ is bounded self-adjoint by [F2]'s positive Fourier multiplier. [F2, step 2.2, algebra]

4.1 If $Hu=-\kappa^2u$, then $(H_0+\kappa^2)u=Wu$. Put $f=su$. If $f=0$, invertibility of $H_0+\kappa^2$ forces $u=0$; hence a nonzero eigenvector gives $f\ne0$ and $$K_\kappa f=sR_\kappa s(su)=sR_\kappa Wu=su=f.$$ Conversely, if $K_\kappa f=f$ with $f\ne0$, set $u=R_\kappa s f$. Then $su=K_\kappa f=f$, so $(H_0+\kappa^2)u=sf=Wu$ and $Hu=-\kappa^2u$. These maps are inverse because $R_\kappa W u=u$ for an eigenvector and $sR_\kappa s f=f$ for a $1$-eigenvector; therefore the eigenspaces are isomorphic. [F2, step 3.1, algebra]

4.2 Let $A=(H_0+\kappa^2)^{1/2}$, which maps $H^1$ bijectively onto $L^2$ by [A1] and Fourier calculus, and put $T=sA^{-1}$. Then $TT^*=K_\kappa$. The compactness of $K_\kappa$ implies $T$ is compact: for finite-rank spectral projections $P_n$ of $K_\kappa$ increasing to its support, $$\|(I-P_n)T\|^2=\|(I-P_n)K_\kappa(I-P_n)\|\longrightarrow0,$$ so $T$ is an operator-norm limit of the finite-rank maps $P_nT$. Hence $C=T^*T$ is positive compact. For $v=Au$, $u\in H^1$, the exact form identity is $$q_H[u]+\kappa^2\|u\|^2=\|v\|^2-\|Tv\|^2 =\langle(I-C)v,v\rangle.$$ The maps $u\mapsto v$ and $v\mapsto A^{-1}v$ are inverse bijections. [A1, F3, step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 The maximal dimension of a linear subspace on which the right side of the form identity in step 4.2 is strictly negative equals $\operatorname{rank}E_C((1,\infty))$: that spectral subspace is negative for $I-C$, and any subspace of larger dimension contains a nonzero vector orthogonal to it, where the spectral integral of $1-C$ is nonnegative. By [F4], this rank is the number of eigenvalues of $C$ above $1$, with multiplicity. [F3, F4, step 4.2, algebra]

6.1 The same maximal negative dimension equals $\operatorname{rank}E_H(( -\infty,-\kappa^2))$ by [F3]: the spectral range below the threshold is supported in $[-M,-\kappa^2)$ by step 1.1, so it lies in the form domain and is strictly negative for the shifted form. Any larger subspace has a nonzero vector in its orthogonal complement, where the shifted form is nonnegative. Step 5.1 makes this rank finite; its finite-dimensional spectral range therefore consists of eigenvectors, so its dimension is the number of eigenvalues of $H$ below $-\kappa^2$, counted with multiplicity. No essential spectral point lies strictly below $-\kappa^2$: a sufficiently small interval around any such point has finite-rank projection as a subprojection of $E_H(( -\infty,-\kappa^2))$, contrary to [F6]. Hence the essential threshold is at least $-\kappa^2$ (or $+\infty$), and [F7] identifies the same count with the form min-max levels strictly below the cutoff. Finally, $T$ maps each positive eigenspace of $C=T^*T$ bijectively onto the same-eigenvalue eigenspace of $K_\kappa=TT^*$, with inverse $\mu^{-1}T^*$ at eigenvalue $\mu>0$. Thus the number above $1$ for $C$ equals that for $K_\kappa$, proving the asserted count. [F3, F4, F6, F7, step 5.1, algebra] ∎

title: Semibounded forms, variational spectra and Birman–Schwinger — Examples

items.title: Rank-one attractive perturbation has at most one negative eigenvalue
items.design_state: Assigned design item; complete current statement and argument are recorded in its item carrier.
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. On
$L^2(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C)$ let
$(H_0f)(p)=|p|^2f(p)$ with domain
$D(H_0)=\{f\in L^2:|p|^2f(p)\in L^2\}$, let
$g(p)=C e^{-|p|^2/2}$ for a constant $C\in\mathbb C\setminus\{0\}$, and
let $\lambda<0$. Define $P_gf=\langle f,g\rangle g$, using the
first-variable-linear $L^2$ pairing. The self-adjoint rank-one perturbation
$H_\lambda=H_0+\lambda P_g$ has a negative eigenvalue
$-\kappa^2$ exactly when
$$1+\lambda\int_{\mathbb R^3}\frac{|g(p)|^2}{|p|^2+\kappa^2}\,dp=0,\qquad\kappa>0.$$
There is at most one such eigenvalue. More precisely, it exists exactly when
$1+\lambda I_0<0$, where
$I_0=\int |g(p)|^2|p|^{-2}\,dp\in(0,\infty)$; equality is the threshold
case and yields no negative eigenvalue.
items.proof_route: Insert the Gaussian into the rank-one scalar condition, then prove strict monotonicity, continuity, endpoint limits, and the strict threshold existence criterion.

references.title: S. Albeverio and P. Kurasov, Singular Perturbations of Differential Operators: Solvable Schrödinger Type Operators
references.locator: Chapter 1, §1.1.1, Theorem 1.1.1 and proof, printed pp.9-10: rank-one resolvent scalar denominator used for the exact separable model.

items.strategy:
**Given:** [A1], [A2], [F1]–[F4], $C\ne0$, and $\lambda<0$.

1.1 By [F2], $H_0$ is self-adjoint. If $E<0$, multiplication by $(|p|^2-E)^{-1}$ is a bounded inverse of $H_0-EI$: it is bounded by $|E|^{-1}$, and $|p|^2/(|p|^2-E)\le1$ puts its range in $D(H_0)$. Therefore $\sigma(H_0)\subseteq[0,\infty)$. For $B_n=\{p:|p|<1/n\}$, [F3] gives $0<|B_n|<\infty$; the unit vectors $f_n=|B_n|^{-1/2}\mathbf1_{B_n}$ lie in $D(H_0)$ and satisfy $\|H_0f_n\|\le n^{-2}$. If $0\in\rho(H_0)$, then $1=\|f_n\|\le\|H_0^{-1}\|\,\|H_0f_n\|\to0$, a contradiction. Thus $\inf\sigma(H_0)=0$. [A1, A2, F2, F3, algebra]

2.1 By [F3], $$\|g\|_2^2=4\pi|C|^2\int_0^\infty r^2e^{-r^2}\,dr<\infty.$$ For $E=-\kappa^2<0$, the rank-one scalar in [F1] is $$m(\kappa)=\langle(H_0+\kappa^2)^{-1}g,g\rangle =\int_{\mathbb R^3}\frac{|C|^2e^{-|p|^2}}{|p|^2+\kappa^2}\,dp.$$ By [F1] and step 1.1, its zeros in $1+\lambda m(\kappa)$ correspond exactly to negative eigenvalues, each with multiplicity one. [A1, F1, F3, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 If $0<\kappa_1<\kappa_2$, then $(|p|^2+\kappa_1^2)^{-1}>(|p|^2+\kappa_2^2)^{-1}$ everywhere; since $|g(p)|^2>0$, integration gives $m(\kappa_1)>m(\kappa_2)$. On any compact interval $[a,b]\subset(0,\infty)$, the integrands are bounded by $|g(p)|^2/a^2\in L^1$, so dominated convergence [F4] gives continuity of $m$ there. Also $0<m(\kappa)\le\|g\|_2^2/\kappa^2$, hence $m(\kappa)\to0$ as $\kappa\to\infty$. [F3, F4, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 The integrands for $m(1/n)$ increase pointwise to $|g(p)|^2/|p|^2$ as $n\to\infty$. Monotone convergence [F4] gives $\lim_n m(1/n)=I_0$. Since step 3.1 makes $m$ strictly decreasing in $\kappa$, its limit as $\kappa\downarrow0$ equals this supremum. By [F3], $$I_0=4\pi|C|^2\int_0^\infty e^{-r^2}\,dr\in(0,\infty).$$ [F3, F4, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 The function $1+\lambda m(\kappa)$ is continuous and strictly increasing on $(0,\infty)$ by step 3.1, with endpoint limits $1+\lambda I_0$ and $1$ by steps 3.1 and 4.1. When $1+\lambda I_0<0$, the endpoint limits give finite $0<a<b$ with $1+\lambda m(a)<0<1+\lambda m(b)$; [F5] on $[a,b]$ gives a positive zero, unique by strict increase. If $1+\lambda I_0\ge0$, then $m(\kappa)<I_0$ for every $\kappa>0$ by step 3.1 and the endpoint limit in step 4.1; because $\lambda<0$, this gives $1+\lambda m(\kappa)>1+\lambda I_0\ge0$, so no positive zero exists. Therefore a positive zero exists exactly when $1+\lambda I_0<0$. By step 2.1 and [F1], these zeros correspond exactly to negative eigenvalues. [A1, F1, F4, F5, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 4.1, algebra] ∎

items.title: A normalized square-integrable vector can have infinite kinetic form energy
items.design_state: Assigned design item; complete current statement and argument are recorded in its item carrier.
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. For the free Hamiltonian
$H_0=-\Delta$ on $L^2(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C)$ with form
domain $Q(H_0)=H^1(\mathbb R^3)$, it is false that every normalized $L^2$
vector is an admissible finite-energy Rayleigh–Ritz trial vector. In the
$2\pi$ Fourier convention, the normalized vector with
$$\widehat f(\xi)=c(1+|\xi|^2)^{-1},\qquad c=\left(\int_{\mathbb R^3}(1+|\xi|^2)^{-2}\,d\xi\right)^{-1/2},$$
lies in $L^2$ but not in $H^1$, so it is outside the form domain and has no
finite free kinetic form value.
items.proof_route: Normalize a Fourier tail in L² and show its |ξ|²-weighted norm diverges, excluding it from the exact free form domain and the min-max family.

references.title: Phan Thanh Nam, Functional Analysis II, lecture notes, Winter 2020-2021, Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität München
references.locator: Chapter 2, §2.5, printed pp.25-27: free Schrödinger quadratic form on H¹.

references.title: Marcello Porta, Mathematical Quantum Theory, University of Tübingen lecture notes (2019)
references.locator: Section 4.4, Theorem 4.65, printed p.41: the form domain is the domain of the square root of its represented operator.

items.strategy:
**Given:** [A1], [A2], [F1]–[F4], and the Fourier function in the Statement.

1.1 In spherical coordinates [F4], $$J=\int_{\mathbb R^3}(1+|\xi|^2)^{-2}\,d\xi =4\pi\int_0^\infty\frac{r^2}{(1+r^2)^2}\,dr.$$ The integrand is bounded by $r^2$ near zero and by $r^{-2}$ for $r\ge1$; thus $0<J<\infty$ and $c=J^{-1/2}$ is defined. By [F2], $\widehat f$ is the Fourier transform of an $L^2$ vector and its norm is $c^2J=1$. [A1, F2, F4, algebra]

2.1 Its formal kinetic form integral equals $$4\pi^2c^2\int_{\mathbb R^3} \frac{|\xi|^2}{(1+|\xi|^2)^2}\,d\xi =16\pi^3c^2\int_0^\infty\frac{r^4}{(1+r^2)^2}\,dr=+\infty,$$ because the radial integrand tends to $1$ as $r\to\infty$. By [F1], finite form energy is equivalent to this weighted integral being finite, so $f\notin H^1(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C)=Q(H_0)$. [A2, F1, F4, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 The vector is normalized in $L^2$ by step 1.1 but outside the exact form domain by step 2.1. Thus it cannot be inserted into the min-max variational family described in [F3], which requires its subspaces to lie in $Q(H_0)$; the universal trial-vector claim is false. This counterexample concerns domain admissibility and assigns no finite value to the divergent integral. [F3, step 1.1, step 2.1] ∎
